RRSP or RRIF. Section 146.3(6) deems the last annuitant of a RRIF to have received the fund’s fair market value immediately before death, and CRA says to include that amount in the deceased’s income. All of it is income, not half: contributions were deducted and growth was never taxed.

TFSA. CRA says a designated beneficiary does not pay tax on amounts received up to the TFSA’s fair market value on the date of death; earnings after death and before the account is settled are taxable.

Taxable account. Section 70(5) deems the person to have disposed of each capital property immediately before death at fair market value. CRA’s guide says this includes investments like mutual funds. The gain above the adjusted cost base is a capital gain, and half of it is taxable on the final return at the person’s rates.
A TFSA is the only one of the three in which growth reaches a beneficiary without income tax, but its room is limited; investors who expect to leave money often fill it first.

A balanced fund does not carry its own tax treatment. The same units can sit in a TFSA, an RRSP or RRIF, or an ordinary taxable account, and each account applies different rules to the same growth: while you are alive, when you withdraw, and at death. The final return is often where the largest single bill appears, because the Income Tax Act treats death as a sale of everything at once.

A balanced fund held for decades is taxed by the account it sits in, and the biggest tax bill often comes on the final return. Follow one fund in a TFSA, an RRSP or RRIF and a taxable account to the year of death: the deemed disposition, the full RRIF inclusion, probate, the spouse rollover and the yearly tax along the way.
A fund’s return also depends on its fees, holdings and currency exposure, not just on an index.

A large RRIF at death can be taxed at top rates. Planned withdrawals during life, at lower rates, can reduce that, at the cost of paying tax sooner; the RRIF minimum guide shows the required payments.

Comparing CAD 200,000 in an RRSP with CAD 200,000 in a TFSA is not like for like. The RRSP balance was built from deducted contributions, so part of it always belonged to the tax system. At a 45% rate, CAD 200,000 in an RRSP is roughly equivalent to CAD 110,000 in a TFSA. Grow both at 5% for 15 years and the TFSA is worth CAD 228,682, exactly what the child receives from the RRIF. For a lump sum already saved, the history supports neither certainty nor paralysis. Investing it at a record has usually worked out over five to ten years but has occasionally meant a deep fall and a long wait. Phasing it in over a set number of months is a way to limit regret, with the cost of holding cash in the meantime, as the phased investing guide shows. A balanced fund, with bonds beside stocks, has historically fallen less than an all-equity index in most crashes, though not in every year. Where the money sits matters too: gains inside a TFSA are generally tax-free, and selling in a taxable account to wait in cash can create a capital gains bill, as the crash-exit tax guide works out.

For money saved from each paycheque, the record question mostly answers itself: contributions spread over years buy at records, in falls and everywhere between, and pausing them in a record month means holding cash with no rule for when to restart. The waiting-for-a-dip guide tests exactly that rule with new monthly pay.

From 1957 to September 2023, 144 of 801 month-end closes (18%) were records. Five years later the index price was higher after 78% of record months and after 91% of other months; the median gain was 18.9% after a record and 30.6% after other months. So a record was not a reliable warning of a fall, but later gains were smaller on average than after months spent below a peak. The deepest fall below a peak was 45.1% (August 2000 to September 2002) and the longest wait to regain one was 73 months, twice. These are prices only, before dividends and inflation, from one market; they describe a past range, not the next five years.

So two things are true together. A record was not a dependable sign that a fall was coming: most record months were followed by higher prices, because records tend to cluster in rising markets. But in this history, later gains from a record were smaller than from months spent below a peak, partly because “other months” include the depths of each fall, when the room to rebound was largest. Nobody knew in real time which months were the depths. Start the count in 1991 and the five-year picture is weaker: 70 record months, a median gain of 12.2% and a lower price after a third of them.

The model applies one rate you enter to all income added to the final return. Large RRIF balances push income through several brackets, so the rate is closer to an average over the added amount than to a single bracket rate.

The second chart measures each month-end close against the highest close before it. Zero marks a record. Nine times the index fell 20% or more below a peak: the deepest were 45.1% from August 2000 to September 2002, 44.8% from May 2008 to February 2009 and 43.1% from November 1980 to June 1982. The longest waits to close above an old peak were 73 months, from July 1987 to August 1993 and from May 2008 to June 2014; the 2020 fall of 22.7% took 11 months to regain.

The second chart repeats the calculation for every year of death from today to 40 years out, for a child or other heir. The TFSA and RRIF lines grow at the same rate with a fixed proportional gap. The taxable line falls further behind the TFSA over time, because tax on distributions is paid every year and the deferred gain keeps growing until death taxes half of it.

The taxable account starts with a cost base of 70% of its value and pays out 2% a year as distributions, which are reinvested and taxed at 30% each year; the tax is paid by redeeming units. That costs CAD 26,269 over the 15 years and leaves CAD 379,484. At death the unrealized gain is CAD 172,929; half of it taxed at 45% is CAD 38,909. Held in one name, the account also passes through the estate, and a 1.5% fee takes CAD 5,692, leaving CAD 334,883. The reinvested distributions guide shows the yearly part in detail.

The third chart compares a child with a spouse or common-law partner. CRA says capital property transferred to a surviving spouse can roll over at its cost, postponing the gain until the spouse sells or is deemed to sell it, and that RRIF property paid to a surviving spouse and transferred to their own plan can be reported and deducted by the spouse. A TFSA can pass to a spouse named as successor holder. In the default case the spouse receives CAD 415,786 from each registered account and CAD 373,792 from the taxable account, with CAD 226,013 of income tax deferred.

The third chart compares the median price change after record months with the median after all other months. Five years after a record month, the index was higher 78% of the time, with a median gain of 18.9%; after other months it was higher 91% of the time, with a median of 30.6%. After one year the medians were 1.2% and 8.5%, and the index was lower after 44% of record months against 32% of other months. After ten years, it was higher after every record month but one (December 1964, down 2.1%).

These spells are the honest case for the fear. Someone who invested a lump sum in August 2000 saw it fall almost by half and waited more than five years for the price to return, longer in real terms. Dividends would have shortened the wait; inflation lengthened it. The loss recovery guide shows why a 45% fall needs an 82% gain to recover.

This guide follows one fund, with the same return, through all three accounts to the year of death and asks what an heir actually receives. It is built for long-term investors who expect to keep part of their savings for life, and it separates three costs that are often blurred: tax paid each year in a taxable account, income tax on the final return, and probate or estate administration fees.

This guide uses the S&P/TSX Composite month-end closes that Statistics Canada published from January 1956 to September 2023. A month counts as a record when its close is at or above every earlier close in the series. You can widen that to “within 5% of the peak”, change the holding period, and start the count later to focus on more recent decades. The exit and re-entry guide covers the separate problem of selling and needing a second decision to come back.

Those three settings are assumptions, not history. Dividend yields on Canadian stocks were often higher than 2.5% in the past, deposit rates were far higher in the 1980s, and fund fees were higher than 0.5% for most investors. Change them to see how sensitive the comparison is. A higher cash rate or fee lowers every cell; the ranking of the rows barely changes.

What this means for a long-term fund plan

When the index has never been higher, buying can feel like paying the top price just before a fall. The worry has a real basis: every crash in the record started from a peak, and a fall of a third or more can take years to make back. But a market that rises over time also spends a lot of its life at or near new highs, so the useful question is not whether a record can be followed by a fall, but what usually followed record months compared with the rest.
